scenes.title: hook: a flask where the rate equals the count

voiceover.text: This flask of warm broth holds about a million bacteria. Each cell grows, then splits in two, and the new cells do the same. So twice the cells means twice the splitting, and the growth rate is proportional to the count. For this strain, counting in millions of cells and hours, and while the food lasts, the growth rate equals the count. A million cells gain a million an hour, and three million gain three million.

Now some changes. The second flask holds a faster strain, also starting the clock with a million cells. That's y equals e to the two x. The third flask holds our first strain, seeded an hour earlier, so it starts with about two point seven million. That's y equals e to the x plus one. When the clock starts, which flask is gaining cells faster? Make a guess. Here's the twist. Differentiate each count, and only the fast strain gets a new factor in its derivative. By the end you'll know why, and how to differentiate k e to the a x plus b.

Let's graph the first flask. Time x goes along, in hours, and the count y goes up, in millions. The curve is y equals e to the x. From Year 11, the gradient at a point is the slope of the tangent, and e to the x is its own derivative. So on this graph, the gradient always equals the height. At height one, the slope is one. At about two point seven, the slope is about two point seven. Gradient divided by height is always one, and that's our measuring stick.

scenes.title: the fast strain: the squash doubles every slope

voiceover.text: Now the fast strain, e to the two x. Here x is doubled before the exponential acts, so the curve reaches every height in half the time. Think of it as the first curve squashed sideways. This tangent triangle runs across one hour and rises about two point seven. Squash the curve, and the triangle squashes with it. The rise stays the same, but the run halves. Same rise in half the run, so the slope doubles, and the whole curve squashes evenly, so that's true at every point. At height one, the slope is now two. So the derivative of e to the two x is two e to the two x. Every million cells add two million an hour.

scenes.title: a dial for a: any growth per cell

voiceover.text: Let's put a dial on the constant a. Turn it up to three, and every run shrinks to a third, so the gradient becomes three times the height. Turn it down to a half, and every slope halves. Set it back to two, then flip the sign, to minus two. The curve mirrors over the y axis and falls, like bacteria dying in disinfectant. Every uphill tangent becomes a downhill one, just as steep. The height stays positive, because e to any power is positive. Only the slope turns negative. Whatever a is, gradient divided by height reads a.

scenes.title: the early flask: the slide adds no new factor

voiceover.text: Now the early flask. Starting an hour earlier just slides the curve one hour left. Sliding doesn't tilt anything. Each tangent moves with its point and keeps its slope, so the derivative of e to the x plus one is just e to the x plus one. Back to your guess. When the clock starts, the early flask has about two point seven million cells, gaining about two point seven million an hour. The fast strain has one million, gaining two million an hour. So the early flask gains faster, but only because it has more cells. Per cell, the fast strain grows twice as fast. That's what a measures, the gradient compared with the height.

scenes.title: three flasks: the stretch scales everything

voiceover.text: Last change: three identical flasks, counted together. That's y equals three e to the x. Every count and every growth rate is three times bigger. On the graph, the curve stretches upward. The run stays the same, but the rise triples, so every slope triples. That's the Year 11 constant multiple rule: the three comes along for the ride. But each cell grows at the same pace, so gradient divided by height is still one. Only a changes that.

Now let's prove it, with the Year 11 chain rule. Take y equals e to the a x plus b. Call the inside part u, so u equals a x plus b. Then y equals e to the u, and since that's its own derivative, d y by d u is e to the u. The inside part's derivative, d u by d x, is just a, because b is a constant. The chain rule multiplies them, e to the u, times a. Put the inside part back, and you get a e to the a x plus b. The b stays in the power but adds no factor, just like the early flask. And with k out the front, k just rides along.

scenes.title: worked example 1: e to the three x

voiceover.text: Let's use it. Differentiate y equals e to the three x. The inside part is three x, and its derivative is three. So keep e to the three x exactly as it is, and multiply by three. The derivative is three e to the three x. One trap. Don't bring the power down like you would for x cubed. That rule needs x in the base, and here x is in the power, so the exponential stays whole.

Now all three constants. Find f prime of minus three, where f of x equals five e to the two x plus six. So k is five, a is two and b is six. Copy the exponential, then multiply by k and a. Five times two is ten, so f prime of x is ten e to the two x plus six. Now substitute minus three. Two times minus three, plus six, is zero, and e to the zero is one. So f prime of minus three is ten. Check the graph. It's five high there, with a slope of ten, twice the height, as a equals two predicts.

Here's a way to hold onto it. Think of the flasks. a is the growth per cell, so it sets the gradient compared with the height. b is the start time, so it slides the curve but adds no new factor. k is how many flasks, so it scales heights and slopes together. In short, copy the exponential, then multiply by k and by a.
Your turn. Differentiate f of x equals four e to the two x minus one, then find f prime of a half. Pause here to answer.

The inside part is two x minus one, with derivative two. So f prime of x is four times two, e to the two x minus one, which is eight e to the two x minus one. At a half, the power is zero, and e to the zero is one, so f prime of a half is eight. If you got four, you dropped the factor of two from the inside.
Last one. A curve has equation y equals three e to the minus two x. Find its gradient at x equals zero, and explain why the curve is decreasing for every x. Pause here to answer.

The derivative is three times minus two, e to the minus two x, which is minus six e to the minus two x. At zero, that's minus six. E to any power is positive, so e to the minus two x is always positive. Times minus six, the gradient is negative for every x, so the curve is always decreasing. It isn't because the curve dips below zero. It never does.
Next, a strain that doubles exactly every hour has a count of two to the x. Is two to the x secretly e to some number times x? Find that number, and you can differentiate it the same way.
